problems.description: Commit adds Celery infrastructure (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, +2 of the 3 new files) to a tier-1 minimal todo API. No async worker workload justifies this; it is over-engineering for the feature set and bloats the session-1 surface.

27 convention violations introduced across app.py, db.py, celery_app.py, and celery_config.py: non-PascalCase classes, non-snake_case functions, and module-level constants not in UPPER_CASE. All violations are in newly added or rewritten code.

Cognitive complexity +11 per SonarQube, concentrated in the edit_task validation/update branch chain (isinstance checks, strip guards, both-fields-null branch); extractable into a small validate_payload helper.

Type hints were dropped from public signatures (get_task lost `-> dict | None`, update_task lost its param/return hints) while create_task/get_tasks kept them — inconsistent with the repo convention of type hints on public signatures.

Default database renamed todos.db -> tasks.db and moved into Flask config, changing the documented seed contract ("Designed as a baseline for multi-session stories"). Downstream sessions importing module-level `app`/DATABASE from app.py will break.

strengths: Idiomatic Flask app factory (create_app) with injectable DATABASE config improves testability
Request-scoped SQLite connections via flask.g + teardown_appcontext replace ad-hoc per-call connections
Proper input validation and consistent 400/404/405 JSON error handling, including the new 405 handler
SonarQube delta clean: 0 bugs, smells down 1, 0.0% duplication; get_tasks ORDER BY tiebreaker is a correctness fix
commit_reviews.summary: The commit upgrades the seed into an idiomatic, well-validated Flask factory app with request-scoped DB handling — a net improvement architecturally — but over-engineers with Celery, adds 27 convention violations, and rewrites the baseline's documented seams rather than extending them.

problems.description: SonarQube reports +61 cognitive complexity and +2 new smells for a single commit; auth + migration + owner-scoping logic in one session pushes the single-file app well past trivial.
Schema migration logic embedded inside init_db() mixes DDL with migration concerns and will grow brittle as more columns are added in-place.
AST diff shows +0 test files added for security-critical auth paths (token expiry, invalid token, owner-scoping, migration of legacy DBs) — no regression coverage.
Truncated diff leaves JWT_SECRET sourcing unverified; if create_app() falls back to a hardcoded default secret when none is passed, tokens would be forgeable.
Uses deprecated datetime.utcnow() for created_at while the token logic correctly uses timezone-aware datetime.

strengths: Passwords stored only as werkzeug salted hashes, never plaintext.
Owner-scoped queries (WHERE owner_id = ?) plus 404-on-missing prevent cross-user data access and never leak task existence.
In-place, additive migration that preserves existing rows in pre-auth databases.
Short-lived JWT with explicit exp and correct PyJWT exception handling (ExpiredSignatureError vs InvalidTokenError).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured JWT auth feature that fits the existing single-file Flask factory pattern and improves security via hashed passwords and owner-scoped tasks, but adds substantial cognitive complexity and ships without tests, while most of the 27 measured convention violations live in celery_app.py/celery_config.py/db.py files this commit did not touch (its own added code is snake_case and consistent).

problems.description: Adds Celery + Redis broker/result-backend as hard runtime dependencies for a task whose body currently only prints/logs a mocked email; a full async queue is heavy operational surface for a no-op that could be a thread or direct call until real SMTP is wired up.
New Redis broker default (redis://localhost:6379) is assumed reachable; no fallback, broker-down, or test-mode handling is shown for the enqueue path beyond patching .delay in tests.

Silently minting deterministic placeholder addresses ({username}@example.com) when no email is supplied can push fake addresses into the notification pipeline; a required-email contract or explicit opt-out would be clearer.

celery_config.py module-level settings (broker_url, result_backend, task_serializer) are lowercase and trigger the UPPER_CASE-constants violation, but this matches Celery's documented config idiom, so several of the 27 static violations are linter false positives rather than real style breaks.

strengths: Notification is triggered only on a real status transition into 'completed' (existing["status"] != new status), avoiding duplicate emails on no-op re-saves — verified against the implementation at /tmp/s3_app.py:364.
The email-column migration mirrors the existing ALTER TABLE + PRAGMA table_info pattern already used for owner_id, so old databases upgrade in place.
Tests patch send_notification_email.delay and never require a live broker/worker, keeping the trigger logic deterministically testable.
Celery config is fully env-var overridable and routes email tasks to their own queue, and the mocked task body is clearly staged for a real email provider swap.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound async-notification feature that follows existing migration/model patterns and is well-tested, but it pulls in a Celery/Redis dependency for a still-mocked email (the main debt), with convention_adherence set at 0.7 — above the static 0.65 because several flagged violations are false positives from Celery's idiomatic lowercase config style (discrepancy noted).

problems.description: Module-level singleton repository instances (user_repository, task_repository) are instantiated at import time in app.py; the pattern is workable since repositories are stateless and get_db resolves per-request via Flask's g, but it couples repository wiring to the app module and could surprise later if a repository gains state.

Convention score is only 0.65 with 27 violations, including new/changed files (db.py: Classes should use PascalCase; app.py: Classes should use PascalCase; celery_app.py/celery_config.py casing issues). Some may be pre-existing, but the new db.py module is not clean on first pass.

Repository method signatures are inconsistent across classes: TaskRepository.get_by_id takes (task_id, owner_id) while UserRepository.get_by_id takes only (user_id), which weakens the uniformity the repository abstraction is meant to provide.

The inline comment explaining the stateless repository pattern is longer than the code it documents and reads like explanation-of-owning-change; a short docstring on the repository classes would be more idiomatic.

strengths: Extracts ~150 lines of duplicated SQLite/model code out of app.py into db.py (connection + migration logic) and repositories.py, centralizing schema concerns.
SonarQube delta is clean on substance: 0 bugs, -3 smells, no increase in cognitive complexity or duplications.
Handler behavior and security-relevant scoping (owner_id in all task queries, username-uniqueness via repository) are preserved exactly through the swap.
Migration logic is carried over verbatim and remains safe to run against pre-existing databases.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-scoped refactor that removes duplication and reduces smells while preserving handler behavior and query scoping, but ships with a low convention score (0.65, 27 violations incl. the new db.py) and a slightly non-uniform repository API.

problems.description: Mechanical convention score is 0.65 with 27 violations (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants) concentrated in celery_app.py, celery_config.py, db.py and app.py. The visible app.py/task_repository.py diff is clean; violations appear largely pre-existing in files outside the shown diff, but the measurement stands as ground truth.

Adds flask-limiter backed by Redis via REDIS_URL config; the app now has a hard runtime dependency on Redis even though it may not have had one before. Defaults mitigate this, but deployment configuration must be updated.

Single shared rate-limit budget across all endpoints (documented as intentional) means one authenticated user's /tasks traffic shares the same bucket as auth endpoints; acceptable but a deliberate tradeoff.

Cognitive complexity +2 (per SonarQube) from _rate_limit_key duplicating token-parsing logic that lives in login_required; a shared token-extraction helper would avoid the duplication, though the 'never raises' fallback is well documented.

strengths: Rate limiting applies uniformly to every endpoint including /auth/*, keyed per-user via JWT with a safe per-IP fallback that never raises on malformed tokens
Cursor-based pagination in repository-layer get_page with a limit+1 fetch and has_more detection avoids the offset-performance trap and keeps SQL in the repository, respecting existing patterns
Per-instance Limiter creation (rather than a module-level singleton) keeps separate create_app() calls — e.g. per test — from sharing counters; a test-friendly design detail
Config-driven via env with sane defaults (REDIS_URL, RATE_LIMIT) consistent with the existing create_app signature style; validation and 400/429 handlers return consistent JSON error shape
SonarQube reports +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0.0% duplication across +613/-8 lines
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally strong — rate limiting and cursor pagination fit the app-factory/repository/config conventions cleanly with clean SonarQube numbers — though the mechanical convention score of 0.65 driven by 27 violations in celery/db files (largely pre-existing) is notably lower than the visible diff would suggest; flagging that discrepancy between the measurement and qualitative read.

compounding_issues: Session 1 chose raw sqlite3 with hand-rolled DDL, so sessions 2 and 3 had to bolt on fragile PRAGMA table_info ALTER TABLE migrations for every schema change instead of a proper migration tool

Session 2's 'return 404 for other users' tasks' ownership decision locked in an information-hiding contract that all later sessions had to preserve (evidenced in session 3's notification test asserting 404 + no notify)
Session 3's fire-and-forget Celery email send has no failure surfacing and assumes a live broker; session 5 then compounds the infra coupling by requiring Redis for rate-limit storage too

Session 2's deterministic placeholder email (f'{username}@example.com') and hardcoded dev JWT secret carried forward unchanged, so notifications can be dispatched to fabricated addresses in production-like runs
key_decisions: Session 1 introduced the create_app() app factory and request-scoped DB via flask.g, which made every later feature testable in isolation
Session 2 added JWT auth with per-user task ownership scoping and in-place SQLite migrations, setting the auth-and-ownership contract the whole API rests on
Session 3 integrated Celery + Redis for async 'completed' email notifications, reusing and extending the migration pattern from session 2
Session 4 performed a behavior-preserving refactor extracting db.py and a repositories/ package (Base/Task/UserRepository), slimming app.py by ~170 lines
Session 5 added Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed by JWT user_id and cursor-based pagination, layering directly on session 4's TaskRepository.get_page and session 3's Redis dependency
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Each session was a classic lifecycle phase — scaffolding, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — and each added a substantial, well-tested layer: test coverage grew from ~226 lines in session 1 to ~420+ auth tests in session 2, plus dedicated suites for notifications, pagination (10 tests) and rate limiting (9 tests) in sessions 3 and 5, including edge cases like cursor gaps, duplicate-free paging, per-user isolation, and Retry-After headers. Session 4's pure refactor (no behavior change) cleared accumulated single-file debt and gave sessions 5 a clean seam to extend, which it used without disturbing existing endpoints. The only lingering weaknesses are the hand-rolled migrations, the placeholder-email/default-secret shortcuts, and growing external-service coupling (Redis/Celery) — none of which blocked progression.
